regressions.query: Host bundle being checked or updated by the basic update driver
regressions.detailedDiagnosis: The query contains the verb participle 'updated' and noun phrase 'basic update driver'. In Arm B (fieldName only), Jev saw '_host' with no lexical overlap with 'bundle' vs '_updateCheck' / '_basicDriver' which strongly matched 'update' and 'driver'. Once class context was added in Arm C (SPUBasicUpdateDriver._host) and Arm D, Jev recognized that SPUBasicUpdateDriver was the driver entity and _host was the host bundle, completely eliminating the regression.

regressions.query: Extracted package signatures checked before running installation
regressions.detailedDiagnosis: Both SPUInstallationInputData and SUAppcastItem declare identical field name '_signatures'. In Arm B (fieldName only), Jev receives two identical strings '_signatures' and has no way to distinguish the package installation data from the appcast feed item, causing arbitrary / stochastic selection. In Arm C/D, adding class name provides the distinguishing context, but also introduces a subtle lexical trap: candidate SUSignatures._dsaSignatureStatus has strong lexical pull on 'signatures'. Repeated runs showed 60/40 stochastic split.

regressions.query: Key bytes used to initialise the RC4 stream cipher
regressions.detailedDiagnosis: The query explicitly names 'RC4 stream cipher'. Candidate class XADRC4Handle contains this exact cryptographic cipher name. However, Arm B stripped the class name and presented only 'key' vs 'keybytes'. In isolation, 'keybytes' was a stronger lexical distractor for the query phrase 'Key bytes', misleading Jev in run 1. When class name was restored in Arm C (XADRC4Handle.key) and Arm D, Jev unambiguously selected the gold candidate with high confidence (0.79 - 0.85, 5/5 repeats), completely eliminating the regression.
